title: He Won His First Gold at 17 and Coached Manu Bhaker to Olympic Bronze. Jaspal Rana Was 49.
excerpt: India's most successful Commonwealth Games athlete and the architect of modern Indian pistol shooting dies of cardiac complications after returning from the ISSF World Cup in Munich
body:
He won his first international gold at 17. He competed at the Atlanta Olympics at 19. He coached Manu Bhaker to double Olympic bronze at 47. On Thursday night, Jaspal Rana — India's most successful Commonwealth Games athlete and the man who built modern Indian pistol shooting from the ground up — died of cardiac complications at a Delhi hospital. He was 49.

Rana was returning to India from the ISSF World Cup in Munich when he experienced chest discomfort. After landing in New Delhi, he was admitted to Max Hospital in Saket, where doctors diagnosed a cardiac blockage and performed a stent procedure. He did not survive.

"Deeply saddened by the passing of Shri Jaspal Rana Ji," Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrote on X. "He brought immense glory to the nation through his extraordinary achievements in shooting. Equally remarkable was his contribution as a mentor, shaping and guiding young athletes with great dedication."

## A Record No Indian Has Matched

Born on June 28, 1976, in Uttarakhand, Rana was introduced to shooting by his father, Narayan Singh Rana, a 1971 war veteran who served in the Indo-Tibetan Border Police and later became Uttarakhand's first sports minister. It was a household where discipline came with the morning air, and the son took to it with prodigious instinct.

In 1994, a 17-year-old Rana won the junior world title in the 25m Standard Pistol event in Milan — with a world-record score. That same year, he claimed gold at the Asian Games. Two years later, he represented India at the Atlanta Olympics, becoming one of the pioneers who placed Indian shooting on the international map.

Over the next twelve years, Rana accumulated a medal haul that remains unmatched in Indian sporting history. Fifteen Commonwealth Games medals — nine gold, four silver, two bronze — across four editions from 1994 to 2006. Eight Asian Games medals, including four gold. At the 2006 Doha Asian Games, he battled a severe fever to win three gold medals and equal the world record of 590 in the 25m Centre Fire Pistol event. He was, quite simply, the greatest pistol shooter India has ever produced.

The honours followed: the Arjuna Award at 18, the Padma Shri at 20. Both were statements by a nation recognizing that a sport most Indians had never watched on television had produced a once-in-a-generation talent.

## The Coach Who Built Champions

When Rana's competitive career wound down, he transitioned into coaching with the same intensity that had defined his shooting. As India's High-Performance Coach for pistol events, he shaped a new generation of marksmen and markswomen.

His greatest coaching achievement was Manu Bhaker. Under Rana's guidance, the young shooter from Haryana became the first Indian to win two medals at a single Olympic Games, clinching double bronze at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Bhaker's success was the culmination of years of Rana's technical refinement and mental conditioning — the kind of patient, detail-obsessed mentorship that doesn't make headlines until the medal comes.

He also coached Saurabh Chaudhary, the teenage prodigy who dominated the 10m air pistol circuit; Anish Bhanwala, who became the youngest Indian to win a Commonwealth Games gold in shooting; and Chinki Yadav, a national champion in the 25m pistol event. Each of them carried Rana's fingerprints — the emphasis on process over outcome, the belief that mental stillness precedes physical precision.

## A Loss the Diaspora Feels

For NRIs who grew up in the 1990s and 2000s, Rana was one of the rare non-cricket athletes who made them proud to be Indian. In an era when Indian sports beyond cricket received minimal coverage, his gold medals at the Commonwealth and Asian Games were moments of quiet, fierce pride — the kind shared over phone calls between families in Delhi and relatives in London, Toronto, and New Jersey.

His death, at 49, came just 16 days before his 50th birthday. The National Rifle Association of India accorded him full state honours. His mortal remains were placed at his residence in New Delhi for the public, fellow athletes, and dignitaries to pay their final respects.

Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya called it "an inspiring legacy." NRAI President Kalikesh Singh Deo said: "He was a pioneer who inspired an entire generation of shooters to excel on the international stage."

## What Remains

Jaspal Rana's siblings — Sushma Singh Rana and Subhash Rana — are both accomplished shooters. His father's war-veteran discipline, channelled through a pistol range, produced not just a family of champions but an entire infrastructure of Indian shooting excellence.

The sport he leaves behind is unrecognisably stronger than the one he entered in 1994. India now regularly contends for medals at the Olympics and World Championships in shooting — a trajectory that traces directly back to a teenager from Uttarakhand who set a world record in Milan and never stopped pushing.

He was 49. He had given Indian sport 32 years. The range is quieter now.
